claims.text: Low hardness and strength in single-phase equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi are primarily governed by intrinsically low dislocation-pinning capability.
The homogeneous chemical environment of the alloy produces relatively mild lattice distortion.
The single-phase alloy has a low density of effective obstacles to dislocation motion.
Mild lattice distortion and low obstacle density permit easy dislocation glide.
Easy dislocation motion enhances dynamic recovery during deformation.
Dynamic recovery produces limited work hardening while retaining good plasticity.
Arc melting followed by homogenization and annealing can produce a single-phase, simple-solid-solution CoCrFeNiTi microstructure with uniform grains.
The proposed single-phase CoCrFeNiTi solid solution is likely either FCC or BCC.
Controlled aging can induce fine Ti-rich precipitates or other nanoscale second phases in the same alloy.
The induced nanoscale precipitates provide barriers to dislocation motion.
Precipitates force dislocation accumulation and hinder dynamic recovery.
Precipitate-induced dislocation accumulation and reduced recovery increase work hardening, hardness, and strength.
The aged alloy will have higher hardness, yield strength, and ultimate tensile strength than the baseline single-phase alloy.
The strength and hardness increase may be accompanied by reduced ductility.
After identical deformation, aged samples will show higher dislocation densities and less evidence of recovery than baseline samples.
The hypothesis is intended to apply to approximately equimolar Co-Cr-Fe-Ni-Ti under room-temperature, quasi-static loading.
Dynamic recovery may have a different role at elevated temperatures or higher strain rates.

contradictions.description: The boundary states that the alloy is maintained as a single-phase solid solution, but the intervention and predicted comparison require an aged state containing precipitates or other second phases. The boundary therefore excludes the modified state central to the test unless it is understood as applying only to the baseline.
